claims.text: Phase diversity in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling and thermal exposure is governed by diffusion-mediated local chemical ordering.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially forms a homogeneous high-temperature BCC solid solution.
Co, Fe, and Ni diffuse faster than Cr and Al in the high-temperature BCC matrix.
Differences in elemental mobility drive nanoscale segregation during cooling.
Local bonding preferences contribute to redistribution of the constituent elements.
Elemental redistribution creates local composition fluctuations that lower the free energy sufficiently to trigger ordering or phase separation.
Nanoscale chemical ordering and early-stage solute clustering nucleate ordered domains within the BCC matrix.
The ordered products can include B2, sigma, or other intermetallic precipitates.
Moderate-to-slow cooling or extended thermal holding permits diffusion-driven phase transformations.
Slow cooling or annealing will produce additional ordered or intermetallic phases alongside remnants of the BCC matrix.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will predominantly retain a single-phase high-temperature BCC structure.
At temperatures where ordering kinetics cannot compete with the homogeneous state, the proposed mechanism will not produce phase separation.
The identity, kinetics, and fraction of emergent phases may depend on subtle compositional inhomogeneities and local strain.
Rapidly quenched and slow-cooled or annealed samples prepared from an identical high-temperature BCC state provide the controlled comparison.
XRD, TEM, and APT will be used to identify phases, ordered domains, and local chemical segregation.
Observing similarly single-phase BCC microstructures with no detectable ordered domains or secondary phases after both treatments would falsify the proposed mechanism.
